# Serotonin syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Relevant pharmacology > Serotonin syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/ZF0Zg3)

---

## Summary

<u>Serotonin</u> syndrome is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by serotonergic overactivity due to the use of <u>serotonergic drugs</u>. It can be caused by a therapeutic dose or overdose of a <u>serotonergic drug</u>, concomitant use of multiple <u>serotonergic drugs</u>, or interactions with <u>CYP450</u> inhibitors. Onset is typically rapid, occurring within 24 hours of drug administration. Classic features include <u>autonomic dysfunction</u>, neuromuscular excitability (e.g., rigidity, <u>hyperreflexia</u>), and <u>altered mental status</u>. Increased neuromuscular activity can also lead to <u>hyperthermia</u>. <u>Serotonin</u> syndrome is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> but <u>laboratory studies</u> may be used to assess for complications such as <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>. Management involves discontinuation of <u>serotonergic drugs</u> and treatment of <u>features of serotonin syndrome</u> (e.g., <u>agitation</u>, <u>hyperthermia</u>). In most cases, symptoms resolve within 24 hours of cessation of <u>serotonergic drugs</u>. In moderate to severe cases, pharmacological treatment with <u>cyproheptadine</u> may be indicated. Patients with features of severe disease, e.g., life-threatening <u>hyperthermia</u>, may also require sedation and <u>intubation</u>.

## Definitions

<u>Serotonin</u> syndrome is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by serotonergic overactivity in patients with exposure to <u>serotonergic drugs</u>.

---

## Etiology

### <u>Serotonergic drugs</u> [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)




* <u>Antidepressants</u> (e.g., <u>MAOIs</u>, <u>SSRIs</u>, <u>SNRIs</u>, <u>tricyclic antidepressants</u>, <u>vortioxetine</u>, <u>vilazodone</u>, <u>trazodone</u>)

* <u>Anxiolytics</u> (e.g., <u>buspirone</u>)

* <u>Anticonvulsants</u> (e.g., <u>valproate</u>)

* <u>Opioids</u> (e.g., <u>tramadol</u>, <u>meperidine</u>)

* <u>NMDA receptor antagonists</u> (e.g., <u>dextromethorphan</u>)

* <u>5-HT<sub>3</sub> receptor antagonists</u> (e.g., <u>ondansetron</u>)

* <u>Serotonin</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>agonists</u> (e.g., <u>triptans</u>, <u>ritonavir</u>)

* <u>Antibiotics</u> (e.g., <u>linezolid</u>)

* Herbal supplements (e.g., <u>St. John's wort</u>, <u>ginseng</u>, <u>tryptophan</u>)

* Recreational stimulants (e.g., <u>MDMA</u>, <u>cocaine</u>)





### <u>Risk factors</u> [[3]](/library/bWXHPC)




* Concurrent use of:

* Two or more <u>serotonergic drugs</u> (e.g., an <u>MAOI</u> with an <u>SSRI</u>)

* One or more <u>serotonergic drug</u> with certain <u>CYP450</u> inhibitors (e.g., <u>ciprofloxacin</u>)  [[4]](/library/LlYwx6)

* Switching from one <u>serotonergic drug</u> to another without tapering

* Accidental or intentional overdose

* Patient-specific <u>pharmacokinetic</u> and/or <u>pharmacodynamic</u> factors  [[5]](/library/oy10Tj0)





> [!TIP]
> Concurrent use of multiple <u>serotonergic drugs</u>, or <u>serotonergic drugs</u> plus certain <u>CYP450</u> inhibitors, increases the risk and severity of <u>serotonin</u> syndrome.

---

## Clinical features

### Symptom progression [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)




* Onset: acute, typically within 24 hours of administration of the causative drug

* Resolution: rapid, typically within 24 hours of treatment initiation





### Presentation [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)




* Classic triad

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u>

* <u>Diaphoresis</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Mydriasis</u>

* Neuromuscular excitability: can lead to <u>hyperthermia</u>

* <u>Hyperreflexia</u>

* <u>Myoclonus</u>

* <u>Clonus</u>

* Horizontal <u>ocular clonus</u>

* Hypertonicity

* Rigidity (especially in the lower extremities)

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* <u>Delirium</u>

* <u>Psychomotor agitation</u>

* <u>Coma</u>

* Other features

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Anxiety</u>

* <u>Hypotension</u> (due to <u>MAOI poisoning</u>)

* <u>Seizure</u>





> [!NOTE]
> HAHA! <u>Serotonin</u> syndrome is no joke: Hyperthermia, Autonomic dysfunction, Hyperreflexia, Altered mental status




> [!NOTE]
> To differentiate between <u>serotonin</u> syndrome and other <u>drug-induced hyperthermia</u> conditions, remember that only SErotonin Shakes your Extremities (<u>myoclonus</u> and <u>hyperreflexia</u>, mostly of the lower limbs).

---

## Management

### All patients [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)[[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




The goal of management is the stabilization of <u>vital signs</u>.




* Discontinue all <u>serotonergic drugs</u> immediately.

* Provide <u>supportive care</u>; : e.g., <u>oxygen therapy</u>, <u>IV fluid therapy</u>

* Give symptom-specific treatments.

* Determine severity: For moderate to severe and/or refractory cases, consider treatment with an <u>antidote</u>. [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)[[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* Mild: <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>hyperreflexia</u>, shivering, <u>diaphoresis</u>, <u>mydriasis</u>, <u>tremor</u>

* Moderate: <u>agitation</u>, <u>hyperthermia</u> < 40Â°C (< 104Â°F), <u>clonus</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>

* Severe: <u>hemodynamic instability</u>, <u>agitated</u> <u>delirium</u>, muscle rigidity, <u>hyperthermia</u> â¥ 40Â°C (â¥ 104Â°F), <u>multiorgan failure</u>





### Symptom-specific management [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)[[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[11]](/library/yC1duQ0)




* <u>Agitation</u> and excessive muscle activity: Treat with <u>benzodiazepines</u>. 

* Mild symptoms: e.g., low-dose <u>diazepam</u> DOSAGE (<u>off-label</u>) [[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Moderate to severe symptoms: higher starting dose, e.g., <u>diazepam</u> DOSAGE (<u>off-label</u>) and repeat doses as needed [[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Hyperthermia</u>: Initiate <u>active cooling</u> (see “<u>Management of hyperthermia</u>”).

* <u>Autonomic instability</u>: Use short-acting or titratable medications, as rapid changes in blood pressure and <u>heart rate</u> are common. [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)

* Give <u>antihypertensive treatment</u>.

* Short-acting agents, e.g., <u>esmolol</u>, <u>nitroprusside</u> [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)

* For dosages, see “<u>Intravenous antihypertensives</u>.”

* Treat <u>MAOI</u>-induced <u>hypotension</u> or <u>shock</u>.

* Titratable <u>vasopressors</u>, e.g., <u>norepinephrine</u> [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)

* For dosages, see “<u>Inoconstrictor drugs</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>physical restraints</u>, as they can lead to worsening <u>hyperthermia</u> and <u>lactic acidosis</u>.




### Moderate to severe and/or refractory cases [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)[[6]](/library/BC1z8Q0)[[10]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[11]](/library/yC1duQ0)




* Consider treatment with 5-HT<sub>2A</sub> <u>receptor</u> <u>antagonists</u>: cyproheptadine DOSAGE  (<u>off-label</u>)  [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)[[11]](/library/yC1duQ0)[[12]](/library/3TWSqk0)

* Temperature > 41.1Â°C: Sedate, paralyze, and intubate patients. [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)

* Use <u>nondepolarizing NMJ blocker</u> as <u>paralytic agent for intubation</u>, e.g., <u>rocuronium</u>.  [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)

* See “<u>Endotracheal intubation</u>” for preparation and procedure.





> [!WARNING]
> Rule out <u>anticholinergic syndrome</u> prior to administration of <u>cyproheptadine</u>, as <u>cyproheptadine</u> can worsen <u>anticholinergic syndrome</u>. [[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>bromocriptine</u> and <u>dantrolene</u>, as <u>bromocriptine</u> may worsen <u>symptoms of serotonin syndrome</u> and <u>dantrolene</u> has not been shown to be effective. [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)[[11]](/library/yC1duQ0)




> [!TIP]
> Agents other than <u>cyproheptadine</u>, e.g., <u>chlorpromazine</u>, are not currently recommended for the <u>treatment of serotonin syndrome</u>. [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)[[6]](/library/BC1z8Q0)[[10]](/library/Y11n2f0)




### Disposition [[2]](/library/GC1BtQ0)[[9]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[11]](/library/yC1duQ0)




* Mild to moderate: Admit to hospital for <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u>.

* Severe: Admit to critical care.
